strengths: Principled and flexible framework: The paper proposes a unified Product of Experts (PoE) formulation combining heterogeneous models—flow/diffusion generative models, autoregressive models, non-neural physics simulators, and black-box discriminative models (VLMs)—at inference time without requiring retraining.

Sound sampling methodology: Combining Annealed Importance Sampling (AIS) with Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) and Langevin dynamics allows the system to effectively navigate multi-modal distributions and integrate non-differentiable rewards from vision-language evaluators.

Diverse application scope: The approach is successfully demonstrated across several distinct visual generation problems, including physics-conditioned video generation, 3D/graphics-instructed image editing, and complex composition with regional prompt conditioning.

Comprehensive technical details and derivations: The paper and supplementary material provide detailed mathematical derivations for flow-based annealing, velocity-to-score conversion, and conditional flow approximations.
weaknesses: Small-scale quantitative evaluation: The empirical evaluations are conducted on fairly small sets (e.g., 30 scenes for graphics-instructed editing, 12 scenes for object-centric video generation, and 9 scenes for full-scene video generation). Section 4.4 (regional composition on GenAI-Bench) lacks a quantitative benchmark table, relying purely on visual examples.

Choice of baselines for image editing: In Section 4.2, the method is primarily compared against RF-Solver using only text prompts, which naturally struggles to adhere to 3D/depth constraints. Comparing against standard spatial/depth-guided inpainting baselines (e.g., ControlNet-Inpainting or directly cascading FLUX Fill + Depth) would offer a fairer comparison of controllability.

Significant computational cost: As reported in Appendix B, generating a single sample requires 4 to 5 minutes on high-end NVIDIA H200 GPUs (and up to 30 minutes for autoregressive models), primarily due to intermediate MCMC steps and parallel SMC particles, which currently limits practical real-time deployment.

Heuristic nature of conditional coupling: The conditional sampling formulation in Eq. (7) relies on an empirical $L_2$ flow consistency penalty and spatial weighting $\lambda^{(i)}(x)$ that deviate from the exact probabilistic product formulation.

strengths: Principled Probabilistic Framework: The paper provides a clear and unified Product-of-Experts (PoE) perspective for inference-time composition of heterogeneous visual models, including flow/diffusion models, autoregressive models, discriminative VLM scorers, and physics/graphics simulators.

Well-designed Sampling Methodology: The integration of flow ODE predictor steps, Langevin MCMC corrector steps, and Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) resampling provides a sound algorithmic framework for steering generation under complex constraints without test-time fine-tuning.

Versatile Across Multiple Modalities and Tasks: The framework is demonstrated on several distinct and challenging visual generation tasks: graphics-instructed image editing, physics-guided video generation, and compositional regional text-to-image generation.
Aesthetic and Controllable Qualitative Outputs: Qualitative figures (e.g., Figures 1, 3, 4, 6) show that the method can follow precise spatial/physical constraints while maintaining visual fidelity.
weaknesses: Extremely Limited Evaluation Scale: The quantitative experiments are performed on very small datasets. In Section 4.2, the image editing benchmark comprises only 30 scenes (10 images × 3 objects). In Section 4.3, the video evaluation uses only 12 scenes for object-centric simulation and 9 scenes from PhysGen3D. Section 4.4 (text-to-image with regional composition) presents only two qualitative examples and lacks quantitative benchmarking on standard compositional benchmarks like GenAI-Bench or T2I-CompBench.

Limited Baseline Comparisons: In Section 4.2, the only baseline compared is RF-Solver, omitting established image composition and inpainting/editing approaches (e.g., MultiDiffusion, Blended Latent Diffusion, or ControlNet inpainting combinations). In Section 4.3, comparisons are largely limited to simple conditioning variants of the same backbone.

Incremental Algorithmic Novelty: Inference-time score composition for diffusion models (PoE / Composable Diffusion / MultiDiffusion) and SMC/AIS for guided sampling (e.g., Wu et al., 2023; Du et al., 2023; Thornton et al., 2025) are well-explored concepts. The specific instantiation (combining ODE prediction, Langevin correction, and particle resampling) closely mirrors existing predictor-corrector and SMC guidance techniques, with relatively heuristic approximations for conditional sampling (Eq. 7).

High Computational Cost: Generating a single sample requires 4 to 5 minutes on modern H200 GPUs (and up to 30 minutes for autoregressive video), which significantly limits the practical applicability and likely contributed to the minimal evaluation dataset sizes.

strengths: Unifying perspective: The paper presents an elegant formulation unifying heterogeneous generative models (e.g., flow/diffusion and autoregressive models) and discriminative constraints (e.g., VLMs, physics simulator outputs) within an inference-time Product of Experts (PoE) framework.

Methodological integration: The integration of Annealed Importance Sampling (AIS) with Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) particle filtering provides a well-motivated mechanism for sampling from multimodal composed distributions without model retraining.

Versatile application domains: The framework is demonstrated on several distinct and challenging tasks, including 3D graphics-guided object insertion, physics-guided video generation, and regional compositional text-to-image synthesis.
weaknesses: Very limited evaluation scale: The empirical evaluation is conducted on unusually small datasets. The graphics-instructed editing is tested on only 30 scenes (10 images × 3 objects), and the video generation tasks are evaluated on only 12 object-centric scenes and 9 full-scene simulations. This limited sample size makes it difficult to draw statistically rigorous conclusions.

Gap between theory and practical instantiation: While the general framework introduces SMC with particle resampling for discriminative experts, the image editing (Section 4.2) and video generation (Section 4.3) experiments are run with particle count $L=1$ and without conditional sampling updates in video due to compute/memory limits. In those settings, the method largely reduces to spatial velocity blending and Langevin correction, which closely resembles prior work such as MultiDiffusion and Composable Diffusion.

Heuristic nature of conditional expert formulation: The conditional flow approximation in Eq. (7) and Appendix D.2 relies on an ad-hoc heuristic minimizing the discrepancy between velocity predictions ($\|v(x_{i'}) - v(x_i)\|^2$), which lacks a formal probabilistic derivation connecting it rigorously to the underlying conditional data distribution.

Significant computational overhead: Generating a single sample requires 4–5 minutes for images and up to 30 minutes for video sequences on high-end NVIDIA H200 GPUs. When running multi-particle SMC ($L=4$ or $16$), the computational cost increases substantially, limiting practical deployment.

strengths: Unifying Probabilistic Formulation: The paper presents a principled Product-of-Experts (PoE) framework that successfully integrates heterogeneous sources—autoregressive video models, flow-based image/video generators, discriminative VLM reward models, and deterministic physics engines/graphics simulators—without requiring model fine-tuning or retraining.

Sound Sampling Strategy: Combining Annealed Importance Sampling (AIS) with Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) particle resampling effectively tackles mode-mixing and local entrapment issues inherent to high-dimensional MCMC sampling in diffusion/flow spaces. The use of Tweedie endpoint estimation for evaluating discriminative rewards at intermediate noisy timesteps is theoretically well-motivated.

Conditional Sampling Formulation: Introducing conditional dependency among generative experts (Section 3.1, Eq. 6) via flow consistency updates provides an effective mechanism to resolve spatial and compositional conflicts between global and local priors.

Broad Empirical Applications on Modern Foundation Models: The method is validated on challenging, diverse tasks—graphics-instructed image editing, physics-simulator-instructed video generation, and layout-guided text-to-image generation—using top-tier open models such as FLUX.1 and Wan2.1 (14B).
weaknesses: Small Evaluation Sample Sizes: Several quantitative benchmarks rely on very small test sets (e.g., 12 scenes for object-centric video simulation, 9 scenes for PhysGen3D, 30 scenes for graphics-engine editing, and 50 scenes sampled from MIG-Bench). As reflected by the wide standard deviations in Tables 1 and 2, evaluating on a larger sample pool would significantly strengthen the statistical significance of the claims.

High Computational Cost and Latency: Running annealed MCMC steps alongside multiple SMC particles poses substantial computational overhead compared to standard single-pass sampling (e.g., up to 4 minutes per image on an H200, 30 minutes for autoregressive video generation, and up to 25 minutes for L=32 particles on MIG-Bench). While expected for MCMC/SMC, this limits real-time and interactive utility, and runtime tradeoffs deserve more detailed discussion in the main text.

Heuristic Justification for Flow Conditioning: The derivation of the conditional generative expert update in Eq. (6) relies on an empirical Gaussian penalty over flow vector differences between parent and child regions. While intuitive and effective in practice, its formal correspondence to the exact conditional product distribution is an approximation that could benefit from deeper theoretical analysis.

Limited Baseline Diversity on Text-to-Image / Video Tasks: While the paper compares against relevant baselines (e.g., RF-Solver, SDEdit, Add-it, 3DIS-FLUX), comparisons with other training-free guidance and SMC-based steering approaches (such as recent diffusion SMC methods or universal guidance variants) on the exact same benchmark splits would provide clearer positioning regarding sample efficiency.

strengths: Principled and unified probabilistic formulation: The paper effectively frames controllable visual generation across heterogeneous generative models (flow-based, diffusion, autoregressive), discriminative models (VLMs), and rule-based physics simulators within a Product-of-Experts (PoE) paradigm.

Sound sampling algorithm: Combining Annealed Importance Sampling (AIS) with Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) resampling provides a neat inference-time solution that circumvents path-wise importance weight degeneracy while handling both discrete and continuous intermediate distributions.

Versatile applications: The framework is demonstrated on several distinct and challenging tasks—graphics-instructed image editing, physics-simulator-steered video generation, and layout-controlled text-to-image synthesis—highlighting broad applicability without requiring retraining.
Informative ablations: The empirical section provides useful ablations analyzing the contribution of conditional generative sampling, the number of particles $L$, and the effect of SMC resampling.
weaknesses: High computational overhead: The inference cost is substantial. As reported in Appendix B, generating a single image takes ~4 minutes on an NVIDIA H200, and video generation takes up to 30 minutes on 2 H200 GPUs. Increasing the particle count to $L=32$ takes ~25 minutes per image, which limits real-time or interactive practical usage.

Relatively small evaluation benchmark sizes: Several evaluation sets are quite small (e.g., 30 scenes for graphics-engine editing in Section 4.1, 12 scenes for object-centric simulation in Section 4.2, and 9 scenes for full-scene simulation). Evaluating on larger-scale benchmarks would improve the statistical rigor of the reported quantitative metrics.

Heuristic nature of conditional coupling: The conditional flow approximation in Eq. (6) and Eq. (9)—modeling consistency by penalizing velocity vector discrepancies across regions—is intuitive but primarily heuristic. Further analysis or discussion of potential failure modes when experts strongly conflict would strengthen the theoretical foundation.

Approximation error in discriminative guidance: Evaluating intermediate noisy states by projecting onto the clean data manifold via Tweedie/endpoint prediction $\hat{x}$ is standard practice in diffusion guidance, but introduces approximation bias into the SMC importance weights that deviates from exact target distribution sampling.

strengths: Principled and Unified Formulation: The paper proposes a coherent Product-of-Experts (PoE) framework that unifies heterogeneous generative models (rectified flow/diffusion and autoregressive), discriminative models (VLMs), and non-differentiable/rule-based tools (physics simulators and graphics engines) at inference time without requiring joint retraining.

Sound Sampling Design: Combining Annealed Importance Sampling (AIS) with Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) resampling provides an effective inference-time sampling strategy. In particular, employing per-timestep MCMC kernels that preserve the intermediate target distribution addresses the path-wise weight degeneracy frequently observed in standard Feynman-Kac/particle filtering methods.

Breadth of Application Domains: The methodology is successfully validated across diverse and demanding vision tasks, including 3D graphics-instructed image editing, physics-simulator-driven video generation (both flow- and autoregressive-based), and layout-grounded text-to-image synthesis.

Informative Ablations: The paper provides insightful ablations demonstrating the contribution of individual components, including the conditional flow sampling approximation (Table 1 and Fig. 2), particle budget scaling (Table 3), and the utility of SMC resampling versus independent parallel chains (Table 4).
weaknesses: Substantial Computational and Latency Overhead: The sampling process requires multiple MCMC iterations and parallel SMC particles over full diffusion/flow/autoregressive trajectories. Generating a single image can require 4 to 25 minutes on an NVIDIA H200 GPU, and video generation takes up to 30 minutes, significantly limiting real-time applicability and interactive workflows.

Limited Evaluation Dataset Scale: Several quantitative benchmarks rely on very small test sets: Section 4.1 evaluates on only 30 scenes; Section 4.2 evaluates on 12 object-centric scenes and 9 full-scene simulation clips; Section 4.3 evaluates on only 50 scenes sampled from MIG-Bench (out of 800). The limited sample size weakens the statistical robustness of the empirical conclusions.

Heuristic Approximation for Conditional Flow Coupling: The derivation of the conditional generative expert update (Eq. 6 and Eq. 9 in Appendix C.3) relies on heuristic assumptions (modeling conditional flow agreement via a Gaussian penalty on velocity differences with a stop-gradient operator) rather than an exact score/flow combination, which lacks formal convergence or error bound guarantees.

Under-explored Handling of Severe Expert Conflicts: Product distributions are inherently sensitive to mode mismatch or conflicting constraints between experts. While the authors briefly acknowledge this in the limitations, the paper lacks an empirical analysis or characterization of failure modes when expert priors strongly disagree.
